newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Up to ASEAN to decide its Burma ties, Britain says.
newsitem.headline: Up to ASEAN to decide its Burma ties, Britain says.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said on Wednesday it was up to ASEAN to decide its relationship with Burma.

Rifkind, in Singapore for meetings between ministers from the seven-nation Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and the European Union (EU), said Europe had already made clear its views on the government in Rangoon.

Burma is expected to be a key issue at the ASEAN-EU meetings with European politicians facing pressure back home since last year's crackdown by Burma's military government on the country's pro-democracy movement.

The London-based human rights group Amnesty International said on Wednesday political repression and human rights violations in Burma last year reached their highest levels since the suppression of a popular uprising at the end of the 1980s.
An Amnesty report called on ASEAN to end its policy of "constructive engagement" with Rangoon.
Asked if Britain supported Amnesty's call for an end to the policy, Rifkind told a joint news conference with Singapore Foreign Minister Shanmugam Jayakumar:
"It is a matter for ASEAN to decide what relationship it wishes to have with Burma.
"We have sought to impress upon the government in Rangoon the need to initiate democratic reforms and to open up their society," he told reporters.
ASEAN groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
ASEAN, which says constructive engagement will bring about reforms in Burma, has agreed to admit Burma as a member along with Laos and Cambodia some time in the future.
But the Amnesty report said ASEAN countries needed to think again about how to press the Burmese authorities to improve their human rights record.
Rifkind said it was important for ASEAN and European countries to focus on areas of agreement rather than differences at this week's meetings.
"Of course there are sensitive political issues but I believe that all countries will be wishing to address these constructively," he said.

"I believe that the links between Europe and Southeast Asia at this particular moment are very, very strong and I believe that there is a common interest to concentrate on the very wide areas where we can have economic and social progress.
"Over the next few days, we look forward to a very successful ASEAN-Europe meeting," he added.
Rifkind said Britain's links with Asia would continue after Britain handed over control of Hong Kong to China at midnight on June 30 this year.
"Our links with Asia are strong. They will continue to be strong for many years to come," he said.
"We will continue to have a deep involvement in Hong Kong through our economic links, through our obligation to watch carefully the development of Hong Kong in the months and years to come," he said.
